doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Collecting cover quotes and the 1961 Village Vanguard recordings
summary: He got quotes from Miles, Cannonball, Shearing and Jamal, then recorded Evans live with LaFaro days before LaFaro's death.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Ahmad Jamal feeling positive about Bill Evans. Well the nice thing see about going out after those quotes, it so happens I got four quotes out of four people. But if it had taken eight or ten people to come up with the four good quotes nobody would have known that when the record came out. But those were the only four people, and as I say Miles’ quote was in existence. Getting a quote from him might have been another whole thing but I didn’t have to. I just would say Miles I’m going to use this, okay? And I called Jamal, who I did not know at all at that time, and told him what I was doing and asked if he’d like to participate and he said sure. Because he did feel strongly about it. But of all people to do that to, I mean this definite self-denying Bill Evans. When he found out what I was doing his only reaction was to say to me — because Bill had a very wicked sense of humor — he says, “why didn’t you get a quote from my mother?” That record made a lot of noise, and of course very shortly after that he had the incredible brief good fortune of involving himself with Scott LaFaro, who was not only a magnificent bass player but he and Bill had a musical affinity that there’s no point in trying to describe it because it’s there on several records. And that of course, if you want to talk about serendipity the recording at the Village Vanguard of that Bill Evans Trio, Paul and Scott and Bill, was — well you’ve got to believe in something — good fairies or whatever — but first of all I had recorded, I’d done two studio recordings with that trio. But I knew what was always true was it took forever to get Bill to agree to go into the studio. Actually the second studio record had been done just a couple of months before that. It wasn’t time to record again, but I said it was a great opportunity where I can set up, record him live, takes a lot of the pressure — I don’t have to ask him to go into the studio, I don’t have to push on him that way. So we set that up and actually the way it worked out we knew we wanted to do a Sunday because in those days the Sunday matinee was a firm part of the jazz week. So by going in there on one day you got two whole shows, the Sunday matinee and the Sunday evening. What we did was we were working on the last Sunday of a three week engagement. The engagements of that length also were the norm at that point. We are now in 1961 we’re talking, right? So we go in there on what turns out to be the last day of the gig. But not only is it the last day of the gig, that’s the last time that trio ever worked together because ten days later Scottie is killed in a car accident. So one of the favorite spooky things about that is during the first afternoon set, during I think the second number of the first afternoon set, there is a brief power outage and we lost about a minute and a half out of a tune. But nobody ever found out what caused it. It never recurred. We could have very easily said oh shit, the power went out, we weren’t able to record that day. And boy would that have been a loss. But we did this thing, we did it at what turned out to be the last possible moment. That’s such a legendary and famous record that a year ago in the spring of 2001 when we were approaching the 40th © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

anniversary of that recording, I got a call from a New Yorker writer, Adam Gopnick. I was interviewed, Paul was interviewed, Lorraine Gordon, who incidentally is the woman who I obliquely referred to under her first married name, the woman who was originally married to Alfred Lion at Blue Note ended up being married to the widower and now, for a number of years the owner of the Village Vanguard. So Lorraine was the best they could do in terms of dealing with the Vanguard thing. So I got to be quoted in the New Yorker as a result of having recorded Bill Evans. I mean that is really fame, isn’t it? Isn’t that really recognition?
